title: Clostridium tetani
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: A soil‑borne, spore‑forming anaerobe that releases a neurotoxin blocking inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing generalized muscle rigidity and spasms. Rapid recognition and prompt antitoxin and antibiotics are lifesaving.

sections.p: Clostridium tetani is a gram‑positive, obligate anaerobe that forms hardy spores. It thrives in soil, manure and animal faeces and enters the body through contaminated wounds.
The organism is rod‑shaped, non‑motile, and produces a tetanus toxin (TeNT) that binds presynaptic membranes and blocks GABA and glycine release.
b: TeNT is a single polypeptide of 150 kDa

t.b: Is the organism present? A positive culture confirms tetanus but a negative does not exclude it because the toxin is already released.

sections.p: Spores enter via puncture or laceration, germinate in hypoxic tissue, and produce toxin. The life cycle is completed in the host; spores are shed in faeces and soil.
b: Common in rural areas with animal contact
Wound contamination is the main route

t.b: Does the wound have necrotic tissue or is it deep and dirty? A dirty, deep wound is high risk.

sections.p: Tetanus is characterised by trismus, opisthotonus, risus sardonicus and generalized rigidity. The toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmission, leading to sustained muscle contraction.
b: Classic signs: lockjaw, jaw spasms, neck rigidity
Severity graded by Modified Tetanus Severity Score (MTS) 1–5

t.b: Assesses respiratory compromise, autonomic instability and muscle rigidity; a score ≥4 indicates need for ICU.

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis is based on history of wound and classic signs. Laboratory confirmation is rarely needed but can be supportive.
b: No specific lab test for toxin

t.b: Shows previous immunisation; <0.1 IU/mL indicates susceptibility.

sections.p: Immediate administration of human tetanus immunoglobulin (HTIG) neutralises unbound toxin, followed by penicillin or metronidazole to eradicate the organism. Supportive care includes benzodiazepines for spasms and airway protection.

t.b: Reduce muscle spasms; a normal response is decreased rigidity.
Eradicates the organism; a rash or anaphylaxis would indicate avoidance.

sections.p: Remember that a negative culture does not rule out tetanus. In low‑resource settings, focus on wound care, HTIG and benzodiazepines. Autonomic instability is a red flag for ICU transfer.

t.b: Signs: tachycardia, hypertension, sweating; indicates severe tetanus.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe muscle rigidity with respiratory failure

faq.q: What is the most common source of C. tetani infection in East Africa?
faq.a: Contaminated animal wounds, especially from livestock and poultry, and deep puncture injuries in rural settings.
Yes, by completing the WHO tetanus immunisation schedule and revaccinating every 10 years.

faq.q: Why is penicillin used instead of clindamycin?
faq.a: Penicillin is the first‑line antibiotic for C. tetani; clindamycin is reserved for penicillin‑allergic patients but has less bactericidal activity.

exam: A 25‑year‑old farmer presents with jaw stiffness and neck rigidity after a foot puncture. What is the first step in management? — Give HTIG immediately, then antibiotics and benzodiazepines.
A patient with tetanus develops sudden tachycardia and sweating. What is the most likely complication? — Autonomic dysfunction; monitor BP and give beta‑blocker if needed.
Why is a negative wound culture not enough to rule out tetanus? — The toxin is released before the organism is cultured; clinical picture is decisive.
Which antibiotic is preferred for tetanus in a patient with penicillin allergy? — Clindamycin, but monitor for efficacy.
What bedside sign indicates impending respiratory failure in tetanus? — Trismus with inability to open mouth fully and difficulty swallowing.
How does tetanus toxin cause muscle spasms? — It blocks GABA and glycine release at the neuromuscular junction, leading to unchecked excitatory transmission.
